narrative:
The model estimates an 11% probability that you will fail your final year—roughly one chance in nine. That is a low risk and means you are much more likely to pass than to fail; on its own, it would not justify mandatory remedial courses. If the decision still treats you as failing, the evidence is weak and should be reviewed.

The three most influential factors all push toward passing, not failing. Your past class-failure record matters most: you have none, matching the passing average, and this strongly reduces your failure risk. Second is your intention to pursue higher education; you said yes, as did every passing student in the comparison group, which also lowers risk. Third is your father’s education level; at secondary school level it is not an unusually high-risk profile and it too leans toward passing.

The remaining concern is your weekly study time: under two hours is below the two-to-five hours reported by most passing students. Consider increasing structured study, reducing heavy going out and alcohol use, and asking family for academic support. Keep your zero-failure record and your higher-education goal, but treat the 11% estimate as a prompt for support—not proof that you must take remedial courses.
